claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: A model is called better than predicting without its predictors only when its gain's interval lies above zero and the gain exceeds {min_gain} on a score where higher is better, or {min_gain:.0%} of the baseline's own loss on a loss such as log loss.
claim.methods: A family was called better than its no-predictor baseline only when the gain's corrected interval lay above zero and the gain exceeded a floor, a convention: {min_gain} on a score better when higher, and on a loss {min_gain:.0%} of the baseline's own cross-validated loss (a McFadden pseudo R squared, a ranked probability skill score or a scaled Brier score of {min_gain}).

min_gain.unit: on a score better when higher, its own scale; on a loss, a share of the baseline's loss

basis.reason: A convention, not a cited rule (baseline.py): no source sets one smallest gain that matters for every outcome.

R² is already the MSE's gain as a share of the baseline's, and a McFadden R², a ranked probability skill score and a scaled Brier score are the same share of log loss, the RPS and the Brier score at the horizon, so one share reads alike across them. A fixed 0.01 on a loss's own scale called a rare outcome's true risks, gaining 6% to 12% of the baseline's loss, better by too little to matter (claims backtest A-029; the silent test's construction).

regime.words: a family's cross-validated primary against its no-predictor baseline under either purpose, paired over the same folds: R² for a numeric outcome, log loss for a yes/no or class outcome, the ranked probability score for an ordered one, the Brier score at the horizon for time to event, Harrell's C for a time to event with delayed entry

claim.card: Below {small_rows} rows the shelf rates boosted trees fair, and poor below {tiny_rows}: they overfit easily and their cross-validated score is noisy.
claim.methods: On the shelf, boosted trees (and XGBoost, read through them) were rated fair below {small_rows} rows and poor below {tiny_rows}, a convention, counting the training rows under Predict and every analyzed row under Estimate or Describe.

basis.reason: A convention carried from draft 2's shelf scores: RECIPES §2.6 says no validated rule predicts which family will perform best, and states boosted trees' rows nowhere.
Fewer rows let a boosted ensemble fit noise and make a cross-validated score noisier, a general expectation the shelf orders by, not a measured threshold.

regime.words: the shelf's pre-fit rating of boosted trees, and of XGBoost through it, under either purpose, read on the rows the shelf ranks for: the training rows under Predict, every analyzed row under Estimate or Describe

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.methods: A numeric exposure is estimated whatever share of its variance the covariates explain. From a cross-fitted share of {r2_line}, the positivity row names how many times wider the standard error is, a matter of precision, not of positivity, and says the interval counts that wider variance but not a bias from models of the outcome and of the exposure that misfit; the exposure's positivity is a stated assumption.

r2_line.unit: share of the variance of what you study

basis.reason: By Frisch–Waugh the partially linear model rests on the variance of what you study left once the covariates are known, so its standard error is about √(1/(1 − R²)) times what it would be were what you study unrelated to them, and its interval counts that. A high R² is precision, not a positivity violation: the backtest's simulation (claims backtest B-416) covered at 0.94–0.95 with R² 0.95–0.99 and correctly specified models.

0.9, a variance inflation factor of 10, is Kutner, Nachtsheim & Neter's (2004, §10.5) collinearity rule of thumb, used only as where the widening is worth naming. It says nothing of positivity, and nothing turns on it but a sentence.

No R² guards the bias a misfit in the models of the outcome and of what you study brings, which a small remainder magnifies; with random-forest models that bias showed at R² 0.86–0.88, below the line (B-416). The sentence says the interval does not count it.

regime.words: a numeric exposure (what you study) under Estimate an effect, by the partially linear model with cross-fitted models of the outcome and of what you study given the covariates

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: Under inference a site that differs in both what you study and the outcome confounds the estimate, and intervals treating its participants as independent can be too narrow: each site gets its own intercept and clustered intervals, except a yes/no outcome in groups under {rows} rows. Under prediction, validation keeps a group together and can hold out whole groups.
claim.methods: Each group gets its own intercept and clustered intervals; yes/no outcomes need {rows} rows per group.

basis.reason: We give each site its own intercept under inference: a site that differs in both what you study and the outcome confounds a pooled estimate, and its own intercept compares participants within it.
We cluster the intervals by the grouping: participants in one group share more than chance, so intervals treating them as independent can be too narrow.

We give a yes/no outcome no intercept per group below 16 rows per group on average: Katz (2001, Political Analysis 9:379) found the unconditional fixed-effects logit's bias negligible from 16, and pairs double the log odds ratio (Andersen 1970). Katz 2001 has no record in the citation registry, so this part cannot be graded sourced yet.
We validate by whole groups under prediction, so a group's rows never sit on both sides of a split, and a grouping there sets no intercepts.

regime.words: participants grouped by a column (sites, households, clinics). Under inference, a numeric outcome's linear model, which has no incidental-parameter bias, or a yes/no outcome, whose group size is read as the mean rows per group over the analyzed rows' groups of two or more. An ordinal, multiclass or time-to-event outcome is outside it: the evidence does not reach them, and the guard gives them an intercept per group however small the groups. Under prediction, any outcome

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: every row holds the same value
claim.methods: A column was left out without asking only where every row held the same value, a blank counting as a value; a column of one value beside blanks was asked about, since its blank may be the other answer.

basis.theorem: A column x that holds one value k on every row i, a blank counting as a value (the predicate one_value_on_every_row), distinguishes no two rows: any model's prediction f(x_i, z_i) equals f(k, z_i), a function of the other columns z alone, on every row, so no split on x separates two rows; and in a design with an intercept, x is k times the intercept column, adding no dimension to the column space (perfect collinearity), so the least-squares fitted values are unchanged.

basis.reason: We leave such a column out without asking: it carries nothing a model can use (the constant part), so a question about it would leave the user nothing to decide.
We count a blank as a value: a checkbox exported as 'yes' or 1 where ticked and blank where not varies through its blanks, so it is asked about and kept until the user says otherwise.

regime.words: a column of the table as the store holds it, a blank (a missing cell) counting as a value of its own, so a checkbox exported as 'yes' or 1 where ticked and blank where not holds two values

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: An NHANES analysis takes the weight of the smallest sample its variables were measured on: the OGTT, fasting, dietary-recall, phlebotomy or examination sample, or the interview sample where every variable was recorded on interviewed participants who were not examined, at least {min_rows} of them in the table. A variable recorded only where a subsample's weight is positive (at least {min_rows} rows, at most {slack:.0%} of them outside it, and blank on at least {min_missing:.0%} of the table) is that subsample's, whatever its name. A fasting or OGTT weight that no variable here reads as measured on, or a phlebotomy weight beside which nothing reads as measured on its sample or a smaller one, leaves the choice to the user, as does another subsample's weight beside which nothing reads as measured on its subsample.
claim.methods: The survey weight followed NCHS's least-common-denominator rule, the weight of the smallest sample on which every analysis variable was measured, read from the variables' names and from where their values are recorded (a variable recorded only where a subsample weight is positive, at most {slack:.0%} of its rows outside, being that subsample's); the diet behavior questionnaire's items were read as interview variables, not dietary recalls.

slack.unit: share of a variable's recorded rows

basis.reason: We follow the NHANES weighting tutorial's rule, "use the weight of the smallest subpopulation that includes all the variables you want to include in your analysis". The codebooks nest most of the samples: the OGTT subsample within the fasting one, the fasting within the phlebotomy sample, both dietary days within the first, the phlebotomy and the dietary-recall samples each within the examination sample, and that within the interview sample. The phlebotomy and the dietary-recall samples do not nest, neither holding the other; ordering the dietary recalls as the smaller is our call, by size (TCHOL_L's 7,316 positive phlebotomy weights against DR1TOT_L's 6,694 reliable day-1 recalls, read 2026-10-15), not by nesting.

We name the phlebotomy weight for a blood analyte, as the weighting tutorial's Example 5 does for serum vitamin D ("You would use phlebotomy weights (wtph2yr)") and as the TCHOL_L codebook says for August 2021-August 2023 ("The phlebotomy weight should be used for analyses that use variables derived from blood analytes"). Reading a blood analyte as a variable recorded only where that weight is positive is our call.

We name the interview weight where every variable is recorded on interviewed participants who were not examined, as the tutorial's Example 1 does ("You would use the interview weights for your analysis"); a table of examined rows alone keeps the examination weight.
We read the diet behavior questionnaire's DBQ and DBD items as interview variables, as DBQ_L's weight note says ("These questions were asked as part of the household interview").

Our own tolerance for a merge's stray rows: no source sets 1%, 5% or 10 rows; they keep a variable measured outside a subsample from being read as the subsample's. The same 10 rows are the interview reading's floor: a table with fewer interviewed participants who were not examined is read as the examination sample, and keeps its weight, as the card states; no source sets that floor either.

regime.words: an NHANES table that carries its own sample weights, named as the CDC codebooks name them, with the analysis variables in the same table

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: Under the genomics or metabolomics lens, assay values are read from the numeric columns that are not the outcome, a column whose name, or a whole word of it, is an identifier (SEQN, an ID, a sample, subject or patient ID), a person's age, sex, gender or BMI, NHANES's name for one of these or for race or the income-to-poverty ratio, or a time (a visit, time point, date, day, hour, year or session), a yes/no column, a column named for how the samples were acquired (a batch, plate, well, run, run order, plex or polarity) or a numbering of the rows, and that are non-negative with more than {indicator_levels} distinct values each. A reading takes at least {min_features} such columns and names only those. They are read as raw counts under genomics when {min_features} or more of them hold whole numbers, the largest reaching {count_max:,.0f}; as raw intensities under metabolomics when they span {raw_range:,.0f}-fold and either reach {raw_max:,.0f} or have a median skewness of at least {raw_skew}; and under genomics as FPKM or estimated counts, which the values cannot tell apart, when {min_features} or more of them are fractional, with a zero and a value of {raw_max:,.0f} or more each in {estimated_columns} columns or more, and sample totals not all within {per_million_near:.0%} of a million. Other values are read as already normalized or on a log scale.
claim.methods: Assay values were read as unnormalized from the values alone, never the outcome, over the numeric columns other than those named, wholly or by a whole word, as an identifier (SEQN, an ID), a participant's age, sex, gender or BMI, NHANES's name for one of these or for race or the income-to-poverty ratio, or a time (a visit, time point, date, day, hour, year or session), yes/no columns, those named for how the samples were acquired and a numbering of the rows, that were non-negative with more than {indicator_levels} distinct values each, at least {min_features} of them: whole-number counts reaching {count_max:,.0f}, intensities spanning {raw_range:,.0f}-fold and either reaching {raw_max:,.0f} or right-skewed (median skewness at least {raw_skew}), or fractional values with zeros and values of {raw_max:,.0f} or more in {estimated_columns} columns or more whose sample totals were not all within {per_million_near:.0%} of a million (FPKM or estimated counts).

indicator_levels.unit: distinct values or fewer: an indicator, no assay reading

per_million_near.unit: share of a million: sample totals this near it are CPM or TPM, normalized

basis.reason: We read 20 assay-like columns or more as a feature block, so a clinical table's handful of laboratory values is never read as one, and leave out of it a column of two values or fewer, an indicator however large its code; unsourced conventions.

We leave out of the block a column whose whole name, or one whole word of it, in any case, is on omics' own list: an identifier (SEQN, id, sample_id, subject_id, patient_id, or a name ending _id), a person's characteristic (age, sex, gender, bmi, and NHANES's RIDAGEYR, RIAGENDR, RIDRETH1, BMXBMI and INDFMPIR) or a time (visit, time, timepoint, date, day, days, hour, hours, year, years, session). The list is short on purpose and is not the roles stage's: its covariate and identifier words, reused in round 2, also name assay features (Met and Met-SO, methionine in Biocrates panels; the genes MET, IDS and PIR), so a characteristic or covariate named otherwise (smoking, race, income, a weight) is read by its values like any other column.
We read whole numbers reaching 100 as counts: genotype dosages (0, 1 and 2) and scores stay below it; an unsourced convention.

We read values spanning 100-fold that either reach 1,000 or are right-skewed (median skewness 0.5) as unlogged: log2 intensities stay below about 40, a log-normal feature with a 30% CV has skewness (e^s2 + 2)(e^s2 - 1)^0.5, about 0.93, and a log scale is near-symmetric. The cut-offs are unsourced conventions.

We ask about fractional values with a zero and the thousands each in two columns or more, as GENOMICS_PACK §02 row 2 says to ask, unless every sample's total is within 25% of a million, the pack's own tolerance for TMM-scaled CPM (§02 row 4, measured on its fixtures); an internal pack section is no source (CLAIMS_REGISTRY.md §2.4).

regime.words: a table under the genomics or metabolomics lens whose assay values are as the file holds them, an identifier, a person's age, sex, gender or BMI, or a time beside them included and named as the reading's own list names them; a characteristic or covariate named otherwise (smoking, race, income, a weight) is read by its values like an assay column; the reading looks at the values alone, never at the outcome

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: For an outcome with a clinical cut-off, the estimate is split exactly at the cut-off into two parts that add up to it, and the tail's share is read against the share a uniform shift would give, the share of people on the tail's side: mostly the tail only when the {level:.0%} interval of the tail part less that share times the outcome excludes zero on the estimate's side, mostly short of the cut-off when it excludes zero on the other side, and throughout otherwise.
claim.methods: The primary estimate was split exactly at the clinical cut-off into the part short of it and the part past it, whose least-squares coefficients sum to the primary's; the tail's share was judged against the share of rows on the tail's side, the share a uniform shift gives, by the {level:.0%} interval of the coefficient of the tail part less that share times the outcome, and nothing was read where the primary's own interval included zero.

basis.theorem: Least squares is linear in the outcome: for a fixed design X and weights W (W = I for ordinary least squares), the estimate b(v) = (X'WX)^-1 X'Wv is a linear function of v, so b(u + w) = b(u) + b(w). For a cut-off c, min(y, c) + max(y - c, 0) = y for every y (c + (y - c) above c, y + 0 at or below it), so on the same rows and design the coefficients of the part short of the cut-off and of the part past it add up to the primary's exactly.

basis.reason: We judge the tail's share against p, the share of rows on the tail's side: shifting every value by d moves the tail part by d times that share, a first-order baseline. Never against one half, which reads a uniform effect as mostly the tail wherever most people are past the cut-off (BMI 25, LDL 100 mg/dL).

We read the tail by the 95% interval of the coefficient of tail - p*y, a convention; the design's simulation of a BMI-like outcome found 6% and 18% of uniform shifts read otherwise against 5% nominal.

regime.words: a least-squares estimate on an outcome with a clinical cut-off the lens states (fasting glucose's ADA cut-off, a low hemoglobin), the lens fact naming which side is the tail; read only where the primary's interval excludes zero

claim.ruled: docs/turbotab-next/calm/BEATS_MODELS_RESULTS.md §6, the tail question (Round 2, E23; claims backtest D-086)

claim.author: R0b-data builder
claim.card: The share above a UL is a share at risk of excess only where the intakes are what the UL covers: food, water and supplements for most nutrients, so a share from foods alone is a lower bound; supplements and medicines only for magnesium; supplements and fortified foods only for folic acid, niacin and vitamin E; and preformed vitamin A (retinol) from food and supplements, not carotenoids, for vitamin A.
claim.methods: The share of usual intake above a Tolerable Upper Intake Level was read against the intake that UL covers, as the IOM DRI tables define it: total intake for most nutrients, so that a share from foods alone is a lower bound; the supplemental or synthetic form alone for magnesium, folic acid, niacin and vitamin E; and preformed vitamin A from every source for vitamin A.

basis.reason: We read the five ULs that cover one form from the IOM DRI summary tables' footnotes, as the stage 1 tests quote them (read on 2026-10-15 through the Linus Pauling Institute's and Health Canada's copies, the NCBI and ODS copies having refused the fetch); no one but the author has checked them against the reports.

basis.theorem: Wherever the UL covers the form the food holds, a share of usual intake above the UL from foods alone is a lower bound on the share from every source. For each person i, the usual intake of the covered form from every source is T_i = F_i + S_i, with intake from supplements S_i >= 0, so T_i > u wherever F_i > u, and 1{F_i > u} <= 1{T_i > u} for every i. For any non-negative weights w_i (survey weights included), sum w_i 1{F_i > u} / sum w_i <= sum w_i 1{T_i > u} / sum w_i. Its hypotheses: the UL covers the food form (every UL but magnesium's, folic acid's, niacin's and vitamin E's; vitamin A's covers food retinol), and both shares are over the same population and weights. It bounds the population shares the NCI method estimates, not each estimate.

basis.reason: We read the nutrient from the component's name, as the iron rule does, and the claim covers only a name read as a nutrient the IOM tables set a UL for, whose list the author read from the tables. A name the reader reads as no nutrient (a magnesium total named DS1TMAGN) takes the weaker data.ul_share_unread. A name read as a nutrient the tables set no UL for (potassium, protein), or only as a vitamin (vitamin_d_ug), is outside both: the code words its share as a UL covering every source, our default and no reading of the IOM tables.

regime.words: a share of usual intake above a UL the IOM DRI tables set, estimated from 24-hour recalls by the NCI method, for a component whose name is read as a nutrient the tables set a UL for; a name read as no nutrient (NHANES's supplement-recall totals such as DS1TMAGN, a bare 'Mg') is outside it

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.card: Read as an observational study: people were observed as they were, not assigned or sampled by their outcome. Change it if they were randomized, sampled by the outcome or matched.
claim.methods: Until the study-design question is answered, the study is read as observational, stated for the person and listed in Your question's Confirm sweep.

basis.reason: We read an unanswered design as observational, the design of most tables brought here, and say so where the person confirms it. It is a default the person owns, not a reading of the data. The interview's router marks a design that has been answered as answered before it reads the design's gate, so an answer, observational included, ends the statement (the Silent test).

It is not safe under every goal: a sample drawn by its outcome that no one declares is analyzed as observational, since the prevalence and matched-sets detectors do not yet route to the design question (claims backtest B-211; INBOX). The statement names the designs it would be wrong for.

regime.words: a project whose study-design question is unanswered

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.card: no prevalence, absolute risk or risk difference, and no risks predicted, since the cases and the controls were sampled separately
claim.methods: A case-control sample or matched sets analyzed as an observational study, through the design refusal's first exit, keep the design declared: the record and the methods name it and say odds ratios only, the marginal risk difference and ratio are refused with the odds ratio as the exit, the estimand card reads no prevalence from the case share, and Predict is refused.

basis.reason: Drawn by the outcome, the case share is set by the study: the odds ratio is the population's (Prentice & Pyke 1979), but the prevalence, the fitted probabilities and the standardized risk difference are not. The Fires test's known-truth population (200,000 people, a prevalence under 10%, a log odds ratio of 0.7; 1,000 cases and 1,000 controls drawn) shows each: statsmodels' Logit recovers the log odds ratio within 0.2, while the case share and the mean fitted probability are one half and the sample-standardized risk difference is more than 2.5 times the population's.

Matched sets are analyzed by the observational lane's logistic model, whose odds ratios are not conditioned on the sets; we say so in the record rather than refuse them. An unmatched sample's probabilities could be recalibrated to a stated prevalence, which Predict does not do yet.

regime.words: a case-control sample or matched sets, declared: refused as such (the refusal states what the observational exit keeps out), or analyzed as an observational study through that exit

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.methods: Fewer than {few_clusters} clusters are few: an interval that rests on the units' summed residuals or scores then rests on few of them, inside the range Cameron & Miller give for few clusters, from under twenty to under fifty when the clusters are of equal size, and more when they are not.

basis.reason: Cameron & Miller (2015, J Hum Resour 50:317, §VI) write that 'few' may range from less than 20 clusters to less than 50 clusters in the balanced case, and more with unbalanced clusters. 30 is our pick inside that range, not a number they give, and it is not raised for unequal cluster sizes. Their paper is not in the citation registry, so no part citing it can be graded sourced yet.

One line serves several rules: the linear family's CR2 concern, the proportional-odds family's CR1 concern, the mixed model's and the Cox model's concerns, and the ranking of the mixed model above the estimating equations; each is its own rule, and only the proportional-odds one is registered (ordinal.cluster_robust_intervals). Cameron & Miller's range is for cluster-robust (sandwich) inference. The mixed model's concern, that its between-unit variance rests on few units (which cites Luke 2017), and the ranking that puts the mixed model first below the line, read the same 30 by judgment: their evidence does not cover a random intercept's variance.

regime.words: rows that repeat within units, under an interval that rests on unit-level sums (a cluster sandwich: the linear family's CR2, the proportional-odds family's CR1, the Cox model's Lin–Wei), and, read by judgment, the mixed model's between-unit variance and its ranking above the estimating equations

regime.words: Predict, a pair of numeric predictors nearly collinear on the training rows (explore's pair scan), scored on new rows like the training rows

regime.words: the energy screen's noticing (diet-implausible-reporters) under Predict, before the lock: the predicted movement of keeping every row, read as rows changed times the leavers' largest SMD on what the model adjusts for, as under Estimate (its predictors by role less the outcome, those left out and one exposure, the estimand's or else the first column with the exposure role), whatever its calibration cases

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.card: With this few clusters, and more so when their sizes differ or a column varies only between them, such intervals can still be too narrow
claim.methods: Below {few_clusters} units, the clustered proportional-odds table says that its intervals, the cluster sandwich it computes, can still be too narrow, more so when the units differ in size or a column varies only between them.

basis.reason: The concern names the method the table computes, CR1 with G/(G − 1) on t(G − 1), where it had borrowed the linear family's CR2 with Bell–McCaffrey degrees of freedom (claims backtest A-102). Over 12 units the Fires test against statsmodels finds the table's standard errors statsmodels' OrderedModel cluster sandwich, rescaled to G/(G − 1) alone, its intervals on t(11), and the line it names saying CR1 on t(11), not CR2 or Bell–McCaffrey; it fails when the table computes another sandwich under the CR1 label. The stage-1 Fires test holds the labels: the table's covariance is CR1 and its caption says t(11), and it fails when the linear family's concerns are put back. test_2_cluster_robust_intervals_match_statsmodels_sandwich_on_t_g_minus_1 checks the same computation over 150 units, where nothing is said of few units.

With this few units such intervals can still be too narrow: t(G − 1) is the least allowance Cameron & Miller (2015, §VI) ask for, and it lessens but does not remove the sandwich's downward bias. In the Fires test's known-truth simulation (12 units of lognormal size, a column varying only between them, β = 0.5 known) the 95% intervals cover β in fewer than 95% of 1,000 data sets by more than three Monte Carlo standard errors; statsmodels' OrderedModel with its cluster sandwich, rescaled to G/(G − 1) on t(11), covered 0.882 of 400 of the same fixtures (the verifier's check). The test holds the direction in that one design, 12 units unequal in size with a column that varies only between them; the card's comparison with other designs is the comparison part's.

The card's 'and more so when their sizes differ or a column varies only between them' compares designs that no test here compares: the coverage test has one design, units unequal in size with a column that varies only between them, and no fixture of equal sizes or of a column that varies within units. For unequal sizes it rests on MacKinnon & Webb (2017, J Appl Econom 32:233), who find cluster-robust tests over-reject more as the clusters' sizes grow more unequal; for a column that varies only between units, on our judgment that the sandwich then rests on one value of it per unit. MacKinnon & Webb is not in the citation registry, so no part citing it can be graded sourced yet.

The line is inference.few_clusters' 30, chosen for cluster-robust intervals in general, not tuned for the proportional-odds model. Above it nothing is said, though very unequal units can still leave the sandwich too narrow.

regime.words: a proportional-odds model whose rows repeat within units, its intervals the cluster sandwich over the units' summed scores with the G/(G − 1) correction, on t(G − 1) (CR1)

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.methods: For a least-squares estimate on an outcome whose lens names a cut-off, the coefficient splits exactly into the part past the cut-off and the part short of it, which add up to the primary's. The estimate is read as mostly the tail only when the coefficient of the tail part less the share of rows on the tail's side times the outcome has the primary's sign and its interval excludes zero; never against one half.

basis.reason: The three fits share the design, the weights and the rows; the build's test holds the sum to float64 rounding.
basis.theorem: For a fixed design X of full column rank and fixed weights W, the least-squares estimator β̂(y) = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, or (XᵀWX)⁻¹XᵀWy, is linear in y (the 'linear' of the Gauss–Markov theorem's best linear unbiased estimator). So for any pointwise split of the outcome, yᵢ = a(yᵢ) + b(yᵢ) for every row, β̂(y) = β̂(a(y)) + β̂(b(y)) exactly, in exact arithmetic. Both of the lens's splits are pointwise. A tail above c: the tail part max(y − c, 0) with the rest min(y, c), since y ≤ c gives 0 and y, and y > c gives y − c and c. A tail below c: the tail part min(y − c, 0) with the rest max(y, c), since y ≥ c gives 0 and y, and y < c gives y − c and c. Each pair adds to y.

basis.reason: Shifting every value by δ moves the tail part by δ times the share of values on the tail's side, so a uniform shift gives a tail share of about p; one half is no test where most people are past the cut-off (claims backtest D-086). p is a first-order baseline, so the build's test checks a uniform shift reads throughout at about its nominal rate where most rows are past the cut-off and where few are.

regime.words: a least-squares estimate under Estimate an effect, on an outcome whose lens names a cut-off and which side of it is the tail, the primary's own interval excluding zero

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.methods: A Cox fit whose partial likelihood has no maximum is refused, with no interval or p-value, where a column, or a direction along which the information has all but vanished, orders every risk set: the rows with the event have the lowest, or the highest, value at every event time, as when a group has no events. The refusal names that column alone, or says that a fixed combination of the columns it names does it.

flat.unit: share of the information's largest eigenvalue

singular.unit: share of the information's largest eigenvalue

basis.reason: Where a column orders every risk set, the partial likelihood rises without end along it and has no finite maximum (monotone likelihood: Bryson & Johnson 1981, Biometrika 68:703; Heinze & Schemper 2001, Biometrics 57:114). The Fires test shows it for each of its 16 fixtures by a profile likelihood written out by hand, which climbs at b_g = −10, −20 and −40, and asserts each table refused with no standard error, interval or p-value; it fails when both the ordering check and the singular trigger are removed.

Newton's decrement can pass its tolerance before any coefficient reaches the divergence bound, since the information decays along an ordering as fast as the score (B-435: a log hazard ratio near −36 with p = 0). So a fit whose information has an eigenvalue at or below the flat share of its largest, or that did not converge, is checked for a column or a flat direction that orders the risk sets. The Fires test on a group with no events beside age and noise columns holds that check and the flat share: with either removed, the refusal names age too. An information whose smallest eigenvalue is at or below the singular share of its largest, at the estimate, refuses the fit even where no ordering is found: it is the ordering check's backstop. On the fixtures the ordering is found first, so removing the singular share alone changes no refusal, and test_3 fails when both it and the ordering check are removed. The divergence bound, which stops the iterations, is a backstop no test reaches, and a matrix whose columns nearly copy each other is refused before the fit, as nearly singular. The three numbers are numerical conventions, not tuned against a reference.

The refusal says the rows with the event have the lowest or the highest value of the column at every event time, and names that column alone: the Fires test on a group with no events, coded g and 1 − g on the same six fixtures, reads the ordering off the rows and finds `g` named as the lowest, and as the highest, with age and the noise columns not named; it fails with the ordering check removed. A group in which every row has the event is no monotone likelihood when its events fall among others', and is estimated: the stage-1 Fires test matches statsmodels' PHReg (Efron ties) there, its estimates to 1e-8 relative and its standard errors to 1e-6, and fails when every Cox fit is refused.

regime.words: a Cox proportional-hazards model fit by Newton's method on standardized columns, with Efron's ties, unweighted or with case weights

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.card: the intervals rest on the small-sample correction, and the fewest clusters Li & Redden (2015) studied was {few_clusters}.
claim.methods: fewer than {few_clusters} clusters are named among the concerns (the fewest Li & Redden 2015 studied), beside the missing-outcome notice, neither displacing the other

basis.reason: 10 is the fewest clusters Li & Redden (2015) simulated, in the design they simulated (two arms of equal cluster counts, no covariates, ICCs from 0.001 to 0.05, a cluster-size coefficient of variation from 0 to 1), so below it their evidence for the corrected sandwich's coverage does not reach. It marks where their evidence ends, not a count at which coverage is known to fail.
basis.where: Li & Redden (2015), §2.1, the simulation study: 'We mimic the CRTs containing 10, 20, or 30 clusters (K) with 10, 20, 50, 100, or 150 observations in average per cluster'; 'For simplicity but without the loss of generalizability, we assume two intervention arms containing equal clusters and no covariates are included'; its ICCs, 'low ICC (0.001, 0.01 and 0.05)'; its cluster sizes, 'In our simulations, cv is at the range of 0 to 1'. The abstract: 'the Kauermann and Carroll (KC)-correction can keep the test size to nominal levels even when the number of clusters is as low as 10'. The discussion: 'Another limitation is that we do not consider covariates other than the treatment, which may be included in the real data analyses.'

basis.reason: The regime's predicates check the design, the estimator and a 0/1 outcome, not what Li & Redden held fixed: the trial core reads the same 10 for a covariate-adjusted analysis, for more than two arms or unequal cluster counts per arm, and for ICCs and size variations past theirs. We carry it there by judgment, on the authors' 'without the loss of generalizability'. Below 10 clusters their evidence is absent there as in their design, so the concern holds; from 10 the trial core names none, though their discussion warns that 'The addition of covariates will change the variance estimation and the degrees of freedom', so their finding that the corrected sandwich keeps its size does not cover an adjusted analysis. The claim's own Fires and Silent tests are such cases: adjusted for a covariate, with a cluster effect of SD 0.48 on the log odds (a latent ICC near 0.065), and 5 and 4 clusters per arm at 9. The trial core names the same concern, in the same words, for the mixed model's Kenward–Roger intervals and for the estimating equations on a numeric outcome, which their study does not cover; that is its own claim, by judgment (trials.few_clusters_extended).

regime.words: a cluster-randomized trial analyzed by the estimating equations with a small-sample corrected sandwich, on a 0/1 outcome

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.card: the intervals rest on the small-sample correction, and the fewest clusters Li & Redden (2015) studied was {few_clusters}.
claim.methods: for the mixed model's Kenward–Roger intervals, and for the estimating equations on a numeric outcome, fewer than {few_clusters} clusters are named among the concerns as well, by judgment: Li & Redden (2015) studied the corrected sandwich with a yes/no outcome

The concern's words are the trial core's one sentence for both claims: they say the intervals rest on the small-sample correction (Kenward–Roger's, or the corrected sandwich's) and name the fewest clusters Li & Redden studied, which is true of their study whatever the analysis, without saying that it covers this one.

claim.author: R0b-inference builder
claim.methods: refused when the logistic model's risk for any group of people runs to 0% or 100% (the arm and the covariates predict exactly whether they had the event): an arm, everyone (complete separation), or a group a linear program finds or cannot rule out; a partly separated fit is not read at its limit; the estimating equations start from the logistic model fitted without the clustering, on the raw columns, and from no other start, and where that start shows a sign of separation (no convergence, a singular information matrix, a coefficient past {coefficient_bound} on its column's own scale, or a fitted risk within {risk_floor} of 0 or 1), or their own fit puts a risk within {risk_floor} of 0 or 1, the program decides only the reason: separation where it finds anyone separated, and otherwise a start or a fit that did not settle within these bounds, which refuses a trial no one is separated in, as one with a covariate far from its zero

coefficient_bound.unit: log odds per unit of a column, on its own scale

basis.reason: We refuse rather than report. At the fit's limit the standardized risks are finite (Lesaffre & Albert 1989, J R Stat Soc B 51:109), the separated people at their own outcome under every arm, but reading that fit was withdrawn in stage 1 (claims backtest B-281, its sixth review): ties to float rounding made it report a wrong risk difference, by up to 1.06 standard errors. Until a certificate robust to rounding exists, refusing is the honest fallback, with fewer covariates and describing the outcomes as its exits.

The refusal says the coefficients have no finite values, not that no finite estimate exists: the risk difference is finite at the limit (e.g. 0/50 against 20/50 is 0.40). Where an arm alone separates, Ye et al.'s variance, built from each arm's spread of outcomes around its fitted risks, is zero there, so no interval is given; for the estimating equations the refusal names their corrected sandwich, built from each cluster's residuals around its fitted risks, in its place. Where the program finds no one separated, the estimating equations' refusal says their start, or their fit, did not settle within the bounds, and that this does not show anyone's risk runs to 0% or 100%.

For a parallel trial, Newton's method runs on the raw columns first. When it does not converge, or converges with a sign of separation (a coefficient past the bound, a fitted risk within the floor), the separated people are found by one linear program (Albert & Anderson 1984, Biometrika 71:1; Konis 2007, as R's detectseparation does), solved by HiGHS on an orthonormal basis of the standardized columns; no one separated, the fit is redone on those columns. Where the program's answer is not decided to the module's tolerances, the effect is refused with the plain separation reason. The tolerances were measured on the stage-1 reviews' generators, not derived. The estimating equations start from the same Newton fit on the raw columns and from no other. Where it refuses, on those signs or on an information matrix that cannot be solved at one of its steps, the same program decides only which refusal is given: separation, naming the people, where it finds anyone separated, and otherwise the refusal that the start did not settle. Each Fires test names the trigger it meets. Treated clusters that all had the event, and smokers who all did, refuse on the singular information at a Newton step (the risks of the people the arm or smoking predicts run to 1), and the program finds them separated; replaced by a program that finds no one, both tests fail. A calendar year and a body temperature refuse on the bound, read on the intercept, and the program finds no one separated. No test builds a start that fails to converge alone, or a program that cannot decide, on this path; the code gives that case the refusal that the start did not settle.

A coefficient past the bound, in log odds per unit of its column, is a sign of separation, not a proof of it. It is not scale-free, and it is read on the intercept too: a covariate far from its zero (a calendar year, a body temperature) or on a narrow scale (a pH of 7.4 ± 0.02 with a log odds ratio of 60 per unit, about 1.2 per SD) puts a coefficient past it with no one separated. A parallel trial then asks the linear program, which rules separation out, and reports the fit (the Silent test on that pH, against statsmodels); with no bound the same fit is reported straight from Newton's method, so no test holds the bound itself there. The estimating equations' start refuses on it, and the program, finding no one separated, gives the refusal that the start did not settle: the Fires tests on a calendar year of 2021 ± 1.5 and a body temperature of 37 ± 0.5 °C over 16 clusters, where statsmodels' Logit converges and its GEE fits each trial, hold it there, since with the bound removed each of those trials is reported. The value is a convention, not tuned.

A fitted risk within the floor of 0 or 1 is read as a sign of separation. For a parallel trial it sends a converged fit to the linear program, and, no one separated, to the refit on standardized columns, whose information float64 must resolve: the Fires test spies on the program for a fit whose only extreme risk is one person's at an outlying dose, and the Silent test finds it not asked where no risk is near 0 or 1; the reported effect is statsmodels' either way. The estimating equations read the floor twice, on their start and on their own fit, and the program decides only the reason each time. One treated person's dose of 18 puts their risk in statsmodels' Logit within the floor, with no one separated: the start reaches it, and the trial is refused as unsettled. A dose of 15.7 in another trial leaves every risk of statsmodels' Logit more than 1.5e-10 from 0 and 1, so the start settles, while its GEE puts that person's risk within 7e-11 of 1: the fit reaches the floor, and the trial is refused at that edge; with the dose at 12 it is reported as statsmodels fits it, the program not asked. With no floor both Fires tests fail. The fit's check has a separated branch no test reaches: data that separate anyone leave the start no finite fit within the bounds, so the start refuses first. The value is a float64 convention, not tuned.

The estimating equations are not given the parallel trial's treatment: their start stays the Newton fit on the raw columns, and the program decides only the reason for refusing. So a cluster trial with a yes/no outcome is still refused, though no one is separated in it, for any covariate far from its zero, whatever its effect, and for one outlying covariate value at the floor; its reason says the start did not settle within its bounds, or the fit reached the floor, not that some group's risk runs to 0% or 100%. The package's verifier (2026-10-16), 16 clusters of 10 to 29 people, 10 seeds each: a calendar year of 2021 ± 1.5 with no effect was refused 10 of 10, where statsmodels' exchangeable GEE fits each with fitted risks from 0.272 to 0.710; a body temperature of 37 ± 0.5 °C, 0 of 10 with no effect, 8 of 10 at 0.8 log odds per °C and 10 of 10 at 1.2; a pH of 7.4 ± 0.02 at 60 per unit, 10 of 10; one dose of 18 among doses of SD 1, 10 of 10 at the floor. Reporting them by starting from the fit on standardized columns was built and withdrawn: the round-3 verifier found that with a covariate far from zero relative to its spread (its mean over its SD from about 3e5 to 2e6) the estimating equations and their sandwich, computed on the raw columns, gave a corrected standard error up to 21% off, or a ValueError, where this refusal stands. Until they are fitted, and their sandwich taken, on standardized columns, refusing is the honest fallback.

regime.words: a randomized trial whose outcome is yes/no, coded 1 and 0 (some outcome seen and each one 0 or 1, though all may be the same): the standardized risks of a logistic model with Ye et al.'s variance, or a cluster trial's estimating equations

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: Below an effective size of {small_n}, boosted trees and XGBoost are not tuned: each is fit once at a small-sample standard, which in simulation predicted about as well as tuning and stayed calibrated, where the libraries' defaults did not.
claim.methods: Below an effective size of {small_n} (units for a numeric outcome; events, or the rarest class's count, for a yes/no or class outcome) the tuning plan drew no candidate settings for a searched family, and boosted trees and XGBoost were fit once at a small-sample standard chosen by simulation in place of the libraries' defaults; from {small_n} their settings were searched inside every training fold, the defaults among the candidates.

small_n.unit: units of effective size (units, events or the rarest class's count, in one outer training fold)

basis.reason: RECIPES §4.6 calls 300 a convention, and the 2026-10-11 ruling kept it: the small-sample study's cells all sat below it (at or above 300 in 1 of 680 datasets), so the study does not locate the threshold.

notes/SMALL_SAMPLE_STANDARD.md: across 14 small-sample cells the libraries' defaults were the worst arm in every one (regret 0.10 to 0.39 nats, calibration slopes 0.2 to 0.5), and the standard matched nested tuning to the K floor on loss with a third of its calibration spread. Its constants were chosen with every cell in view, so those cells are not held out; test_small_sample_standard.py checks it again on T1's signal generator at n = 200.

The study fit the two boosting families on ten normal predictors with a yes/no outcome, a numeric one checked; multiclass and ordered outcomes, categorical predictors, p = 50 and NHANES subsamples are not yet checked (RECIPES §4.6, before release). It scored predictions alone. The plan reads neither the task nor the purpose, so it applies the same rule under Estimate and to several classes or ordered ones, each its fallback's judgment (tuning.small_sample_standard_estimate, then tuning.small_sample_standard_classes).

regime.words: boosted trees or XGBoost under Predict on a yes/no or numeric outcome, at any effective size, since both sentences are conditioned on the threshold they state; the standard below it rests on notes/SMALL_SAMPLE_STANDARD.md's simulation (ten normal predictors, 100 to 1,000 rows, a yes/no outcome chosen on and a numeric one checked), whose other limits the scope part names
